title: The Supper and the Long Night
sum: As Passover draws near, the chief priests look for a way to kill Jesus without a riot, and Satan enters Judas, who agrees to hand him over for silver. Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the meal in a guest room upstairs. At the table he tells the apostles how he has longed to eat this Passover with them before he suffers. He shares a cup, then gives them the bread as his body "given for you," and after the meal the cup of "the new covenant, made in my blood." He tells them to do this to remember him.

The meal becomes a farewell. Jesus names a betrayer at the table, settles a quarrel about greatness by calling himself the one who waits on tables, and bequeaths them a kingdom. He warns Simon that Satan will sift them all, but that he has prayed for Simon's faith, and he foretells three denials before the rooster crows. Then he reverses his old mission orders: now they must take purse and bag, and buy a sword, because Scripture must be fulfilled: "And he was counted with the lawless."

On the Mount of Olives Jesus kneels and prays, "Father, if you are willing, make this cup pass me by," and, in many manuscripts, an angel strengthens him and his sweat falls like drops of blood. Judas comes with a crowd; a disciple cuts off a slave's ear and Jesus heals it. Through the night Peter denies him three times, until the Lord turns and looks at him, and he goes out and weeps. At daybreak the council asks whether he is the Messiah and the Son of God, and takes his answer as enough.
readings: The arrest of Jesus by the temple leadership at Passover, his handing over to Pilate and the flight or failure of his followers are among the best attested events of his life. Historians debate the date of the meal (Passover night in Luke, the day before in John), whether there was a formal trial or only a hearing, and how much of the private scenes, the prayer and the words at the table, comes from witnesses. Luke's account has its own details that some scholars trace to a separate source: a single morning session of the council, the healing of the ear and the look at Peter.

Luke turns the Last Supper into a testament, the last words of a great man to his heirs, like Jacob's or Moses'. The founder gives his followers a meal to repeat, a rule for leadership (serve, do not lord it), a kingdom to share, a warning of trial and a prayer for the one who will lead them. The rest of Luke-Acts shows the heirs carrying out the will: breaking bread, serving tables, and Peter strengthening his brothers.
Read as the hour of darkness

Luke frames the night as a battle. Satan enters Judas (22:3), asks to sift the disciples (22:31), and the arrest comes in the hour that "belongs to you, and to the authority of darkness" (22:53). Against this power Jesus' weapons are prayer, healing and a look of love. The chapter asks the reader to pray not to come into testing, and shows what happens to those who sleep.

views.H: The Passover lambs were killed in the temple on the afternoon of Nisan 14 and eaten that night in Jerusalem, where pilgrims swelled the city several times over. Reclining at table, the cups of wine and the blessings over bread and wine fit what the Mishnah later records of the Passover meal. The temple police under their commanders, not Roman troops, make the arrest in Luke. The council meets at daybreak, the time when a court could lawfully sit, and decides to take Jesus to Pilate, who alone could order a crucifixion.
views.C: Luke follows Mark's order in outline but differs often: the betrayal warning comes after the supper, the dispute about greatness moves to the table, the sayings about Simon and the swords are Luke's alone, Jesus prays once, not three times, the denials come before the hearing, and the hearing has no witnesses or verdict. Scholars explain these either by a second passion source that Luke combined with Mark or by Luke's own editing. Luke's words over the bread and cup agree with Paul (1 Corinthians 11:23–25). The chapter holds two of the Gospel's most famous textual problems: the longer and shorter forms of the Supper (22:19–20) and the angel and bloody sweat (22:43–44).
views.L: The chapter is built around tables and prayer. At the table, the master serves; the kingdom is pictured as eating and drinking at his table. In the garden, prayer frames the scene (22:40, 46) and Jesus kneels between two warnings. Luke softens the disciples' failures (they sleep "from grief"; they are never said to flee) and sharpens Jesus' control: he speaks before Judas kisses him, he heals the ear, he turns and looks at Peter. "Lord" is the narrator's title for Jesus here (22:61), as the end approaches.
views.J: The meal is a Jewish Passover, eaten with blessings over cup and bread, and Jesus speaks of its fulfillment in the kingdom of God, the hope of Israel's prophets. Luke distinguishes the people, who are on Jesus' side and whom the leaders fear (22:2, 6), from the chief priests and their officers. The council's questions, Messiah and Son of God, are Jewish questions about Israel's king. Jewish scholars note that a Sanhedrin hearing at the high priest's house at Passover raises historical problems, and that Christian retellings of this night were later used to blame Jews collectively.
views.T: The church has read these verses on Maundy Thursday since early times. The words "Do this to remember me" are spoken at every Eucharist, and churches differ on what the remembering does (see the card below). The prayer on the Mount of Olives became the model of Christian submission, "may your will be done, not mine," and the Third Council of Constantinople (681) defended from it that Christ had a human will. Painters such as El Greco drew the angel holding out a cup. Peter's tears made him, for the church, the patron of every penitent.

deep.h: Luke's Supper: two cups and a shorter text
deep.b:
The deep dive at Matthew 26 compares the four accounts of the Last Supper and the question of whether it was a Passover meal. Luke adds a puzzle of his own. In the longer text that almost all manuscripts have, the meal runs: a cup with thanksgiving and a saying about not drinking again (22:17–18); bread, "my body, which is being given for you," and "Do this to remember me" (22:19); and after the meal a second cup, "the new covenant, made in my blood" (22:20). The last part is almost word for word Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11:23–25.

Codex Bezae and several Old Latin manuscripts stop at "This is my body," so that the meal runs cup, bread. Other Old Latin and Syriac manuscripts rearrange the verses in four further ways (Metzger lists six forms in all). In 1881 Westcott and Hort judged the shorter text original and the rest an addition from Paul; the RSV followed them. Since then the discovery of Papyrus 75, a copy of about AD 175–225 with the longer text, and further study have led nearly all editors to print it. The longer text explains the other forms best: scribes who found two cups confusing cut or moved one. Bart Ehrman argues the reverse, that the words "given for you" were added to stress the atoning value of Jesus' death against teachers who denied it.

Either way Luke's account keeps something the others lose: a Passover meal with more than one cup, as the Mishnah describes, in which Jesus' words over the bread and the cup after supper come as the climax of the meal.

Ancient Jewish and Greek literature has many "farewell discourses," the last words of a dying leader to his followers: Jacob blessing his sons (Genesis 49), Moses in Deuteronomy, David's charge to Solomon (1 Kings 2), the Testaments of the Twelve Patriarchs, Socrates in Plato's Phaedo. They share features: the leader announces his death, reviews his life, warns of trouble ahead, appoints successors, gives rules for the community and prays for them.

Luke gives Jesus such a speech at the Last Supper (22:21–38), and John a much longer one (John 13–17). Jesus announces his suffering (22:15), speaks of betrayal and of the disciples' trials, gives a rule for leaders (22:25–27), appoints the Twelve to share his kingdom (22:29–30), prays for Peter and charges him to strengthen the others (22:31–32), and warns of hostility (22:35–38). In Acts Paul gives the same kind of speech to the elders of Ephesus (Acts 20:17–38), warning, charging and praying. For Luke's readers the Supper was not only a memory but the founding instruction for how the church's leaders should behave at its own tables.

deep.h: The angel and the bloody sweat (22:43–44)
deep.b:
No other passage in Luke divides the early manuscripts so evenly. The verses are absent from Papyrus 75 and Codex Vaticanus, the two best Alexandrian witnesses, and from Alexandrinus and Washington; they are present in Sinaiticus (first hand), Bezae and most later manuscripts; a corrector of Sinaiticus marked them for deletion and a later one restored them. Justin Martyr, about AD 155, already knew the sweat like drops of blood, and Irenaeus and Hippolytus cite the verses. Some manuscripts mark them with signs of doubt, and one family moves them into Matthew's Gethsemane.

For a later addition: Bart Ehrman and Mark Plunkett argued that the prayer scene forms a neat ring without them (pray, withdraw, kneel, pray, rise, return, pray), which the verses break, and that they were added in the second century to show, against docetists, that Jesus truly suffered in the flesh. For Luke's authorship: Raymond Brown and others note that their words are Lukan, that an angel strengthening Jesus fits Luke's love of angels, and that scribes had reason to cut them, since a Jesus in anguish and needing an angel's help embarrassed those who stressed his divinity.

The Plain prints them, as nearly all Bibles do, and marks them with a variant note. Whatever their origin, they have shaped how Christians picture the night: the cost of obedience written in sweat like blood.

deep.title: Claude's theory: when the light failed, the faith did not
deep.b: Luke uses the verb ekleipō, "to fail, give out," only three times. In 16:9 Jesus says to make friends with dishonest wealth "so that when it runs out" they will welcome you into the everlasting tents. In 22:32 he prays that Simon's faith "would not fail." In 23:45 the sun "had failed" at noon. I suggest Luke means the reader to hear the three together. Money will fail; the sun failed in the hour of darkness (22:53), when the powers seemed to win; but the faith for which Jesus prayed did not fail, even through Peter's denial, and it is Peter's restored faith that strengthens the others (22:32; 24:34; Acts 2:14). The theory rests only on the repeated word and the darkness theme; commentators have noted the eclipse sense of 23:45 and the prayer of 22:32, but I have not seen the three uses read as a set.

echoes: Exodus 12:1–14; Exodus 24:8; Jeremiah 31:31–34; Isaiah 53:12; Psalm 41:9; Zechariah 13:7; Amos 9:9; Job 1:6–12; 1 Kings 19:5–8; Psalm 110:1; Daniel 7:13; Matthew 26:1–75; Mark 14:1–72; John 13:1–18:27; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26; Acts 1:15–26; Acts 20:17–38; Hebrews 5:7–8

settings.when: on the day the Passover lambs were sacrificed, in or near Jerusalem
settings.why: to arrange a private room for the meal, apparently in a way that kept the place hidden until the last moment
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw the two who would lead the church in Acts learning to serve, and Jesus in control of the hour of his own suffering.

settings.what: The words over the Passover, the bread and the cup
settings.when: at the Passover meal on the night before his death
settings.why: to say farewell, to tell them he would not eat or drink again until the kingdom came, and to give the bread and cup a new meaning: his body given and his blood poured out for them, a new covenant to be remembered
settings.readers: For Luke's churches, which met to break bread (Acts 2:42; 20:7), these words were the charter of their own meal, nearly the same as those Paul handed on (1 Corinthians 11:23–25).

settings.when: after the bread and cup
settings.why: to show that the betrayal was known to him and fell within God's plan, while warning the betrayer of its guilt
settings.readers: Readers learned that sharing the Lord's table did not protect against betraying him, a warning Paul gives the Corinthians too (1 Corinthians 11:27–29).
views: Both put the warning about the betrayer before the bread and cup (Mark 14:18–21; Matthew 26:21–25); Luke puts it after, so that the betrayer has shared the cup.

settings.what: Who is the greatest: the servant and the kingdom
settings.when: at the end of the Last Supper
settings.why: to overturn the world's model of power, where rulers dominate and call themselves benefactors, and to promise the faithful a share in his kingdom and his table
settings.readers: Luke's readers, whose leaders were elders and overseers by the time he wrote, heard a rule for every church office: lead as the one who waits on tables.
views: Many think Luke moved the saying about greatness from the road (Mark 10:41–45) to the table to make it part of a farewell testament.
Others think Jesus spoke of greatness more than once and Luke records the occasion at the Supper.
Matthew sets the promise of thrones (22:30) on the road, in answer to Peter's "What will we get?" (Matthew 19:27–28).

settings.what: Prayer for Simon and the warning of denial
settings.to: Simon Peter, and through him the others
settings.when: at the table, after the promise of the kingdom
settings.why: to warn Peter of the coming test, to assure him of Jesus' prayer, and to give him in advance the task of strengthening the others once he had turned back
settings.readers: Readers who knew Peter as the leader of the first church saw that his leadership rested not on his strength but on Jesus' prayer and his own restoring.
views: Both put the prediction of Peter's denial on the way to the Mount of Olives, after the meal (Mark 14:26–31; Matthew 26:30–35); Luke and John keep it at the table (John 13:36–38).

settings.when: the last words at table before going to the Mount of Olives
settings.why: to tell them that the time of welcome was over and the time of hostility had begun, as Isaiah's words about being counted with the lawless came true
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who faced suspicion and persecution, heard that they could no longer count on the welcome the first missionaries found; the swords and Jesus' "It is enough" have been argued over ever since.
views: Most interpreters: a vivid picture of coming danger, which the disciples took literally.
Some: permission to carry arms for protection on the road.
Some: the swords make the group look like outlaws so that Isaiah 53:12 is fulfilled.

settings.what: The prayer on the Mount of Olives
settings.to: the Father, with the disciples a stone's throw away
settings.when: at night, after the Supper, at his usual place on the Mount of Olives
settings.why: to submit his will to the Father's in the face of death, and to teach the disciples to pray against coming into testing
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned how to face trial: kneeling in prayer, honest about dread, and saying "may your will be done"; Stephen and Paul pray the same way in Acts (Acts 7:60; 21:5, 14).

settings.to: Judas, the disciples, and the chief priests, temple commanders and elders who came to arrest him
settings.when: at night on the Mount of Olives
settings.why: to expose the betrayal by a kiss, to stop armed resistance, to heal the wounded slave, and to tell the leaders that their secret arrest belonged to the hour of darkness
settings.readers: Readers saw their Lord refuse the sword and heal an enemy at the moment of greatest danger.

settings.by: Peter; a slave girl and two men in the courtyard
settings.to: the people around the fire in the high priest's courtyard
settings.when: through the night of Jesus' arrest
settings.why: Peter, afraid, denied knowing Jesus, being one of his followers, and even knowing what they meant; the rooster and the Lord's look brought him to repentance
settings.readers: For Luke's readers, some of whom had denied the faith under pressure, Peter's fall and tears showed both the danger and the way back.

settings.when: during the night at the high priest's house
settings.why: to humiliate a prisoner whose followers called him a prophet
settings.readers: Readers saw the irony: Jesus' prophecy about Peter had just come true.

settings.by: the council of elders: chief priests and scribes; Jesus
settings.to: each other and Jesus, in their Sanhedrin
settings.when: at daybreak
settings.why: for the council, to establish whether Jesus claimed to be the Messiah and the Son of God, so that they could bring a charge to Pilate; for Jesus, to refuse their terms while affirming that the Son of Man would reign at God's right hand
settings.readers: Luke's readers heard the claim on which the church stood: Jesus already seated at God's right hand (Acts 2:33–36; 7:56).
views: Many think a hearing before the high priest and his council, preparing a political charge for Pilate, is historically likely.
Others think the scene was shaped by early Christian preaching about Jesus as Messiah and Son of God.

traditions.q: "Do this to remember me" (22:19). Is the Lord's Supper a sacrifice, or a memorial of one? (Whether Christ is truly present in the bread and wine is on the card at Matthew 26:26.)
views: The Eucharist is the memorial (anamnēsis) of Christ's Passover, and in it the one sacrifice of the cross is made present: "The sacrifice of Christ and the sacrifice of the Eucharist are one single sacrifice" (Catechism 1362–1367). By these words Christ also made the apostles priests to offer it (Council of Trent, Session 22, canon 2).

The Divine Liturgy obeys the command by remembering "the cross, the tomb, the resurrection on the third day, the ascension into heaven, the sitting at the right hand, and the second and glorious coming," and then offers to God "your own of your own." The Eucharist is the bloodless sacrifice, one with Christ's offering, and the remembrance includes even the future coming.

The Supper is Christ's testament and gift, given to be received in faith, not a sacrifice that earns grace for others. The Augsburg Confession rejects the Mass as a sacrifice for the sins of the living and the dead (Article 24), while the Apology allows a sacrifice of thanksgiving and praise.

"Christ is not offered up to his Father; nor any real sacrifice made at all ... but only a commemoration of that one offering up of himself" on the cross, and a spiritual offering of praise (Westminster Confession 29.2). The remembering is by faith, through which believers are fed on Christ by the Spirit.

Christ commanded "a perpetual memory of that his precious death, until his coming again" (Book of Common Prayer, 1662), and the Articles reject "the sacrifices of Masses" (Article 31). Anglo-Catholics speak of the Eucharist as a sacrifice; the Anglican–Roman Catholic commission's Windsor Statement (1971) found common ground in the biblical idea of anamnēsis.

The Lord's Supper is "a symbolic act of obedience whereby members of the church ... memorialize the death of the Redeemer and anticipate His second coming" (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, Article 7). It is a memorial, not a sacrifice or a means of grace in itself.

traditions.q: Jesus prayed that Simon's faith would not fail and told him to strengthen his brothers (22:32). Does this promise pass to Peter's successors? (The wider question of Peter and the papacy is on the card at Matthew 16:18.)
views: Yes. The First Vatican Council quotes this verse in defining papal infallibility, teaching that the gift of truth and of a faith that never fails was divinely given to Peter and to his successors in his chair (Pastor Aeternus 4).

The prayer was for Peter himself, who fell and was restored. Strengthening the brethren is the task of every bishop who keeps the faith Peter confessed; no bishop is infallible, and the church's faith is guarded by the whole body in council.

Christ's prayer shows his care for a disciple about to fall, as he intercedes for all believers (Romans 8:34). It gives no bishop authority over the church by divine right (Melanchthon, Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope).

The prayer was for Peter himself, facing his own fall, and the charge to strengthen others falls to every believer God restores. Reformed churches deny that any bishop inherits a promise of unfailing faith; Calvin argues at length against the primacy of the Roman see (Institutes 4.6).

traditions.q: Jesus told the disciples to sell a cloak and buy a sword, and then said of two swords, "It is enough" (22:36–38). Does this allow Christians to use the sword? (The wider questions are on the cards at Matthew 5:39 and 26:52.)
views: No. The same night Jesus stopped the sword and healed the wounded man (22:51); his words about swords were a sign of being counted with the lawless, and "It is enough" ended the disciples' misunderstanding. Christians are called to nonresistance and peacemaking (Schleitheim Confession 6; Confession of Faith in a Mennonite Perspective, Article 22).

Medieval popes read the "two swords" as the spiritual and the temporal power, both belonging to the church (Boniface VIII, Unam Sanctam, 1302). Catholic teaching today does not rest on that reading, but holds that legitimate defense of oneself and others is lawful and can be a grave duty (Catechism 2263–2265).

Calvin took the saying as a figure for the hard struggle ahead, which the disciples crudely took literally; the lawful use of the sword by the civil magistrate rests on other texts (Westminster Confession 23.2).

title: Innocent, and Crucified
sum: The council brings Jesus to Pilate with three charges: misleading the nation, forbidding taxes to Caesar, and claiming to be Messiah, a king. Pilate finds nothing to charge him with. Hearing that Jesus is a Galilean, he sends him to Herod Antipas, who has long wanted to see a miracle; Jesus says nothing, and Herod and his soldiers mock him and send him back in a shining robe. That day the two rulers become friends. Pilate declares Jesus innocent a second and a third time and offers to flog and release him, but the crowd, with the chief priests and rulers, demands Barabbas, a rebel and murderer, and shouts "Crucify him!" Pilate gives in.

On the way out Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross behind Jesus. Women of Jerusalem mourn, and Jesus tells them to weep for themselves and their children. At the place called Skull he is crucified between two criminals, praying, "Father, forgive them." Rulers, soldiers and one criminal mock him; the other criminal rebukes them and asks, "Jesus, remember me," and Jesus promises, "today you will be with me in paradise."

Darkness covers the land from noon to three, the sun fails, and the sanctuary curtain is torn. Jesus cries out the words of Psalm 31, "Father, into your hands I place my spirit," and dies. A centurion gives glory to God and says he was righteous; the crowds go home beating their chests; his friends and the women from Galilee watch from far off. Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not agreed with the decision, buries him in a new rock tomb before the Sabbath, and the women prepare spices and rest on the Sabbath as the Law commands.
readings: That Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate is one of the surest facts of ancient history, reported by Tacitus (Annals 15.44) and Josephus as well as by the Christian sources. The charge, "King of the Jews," fits a Roman execution for sedition. Luke alone tells of the hearing before Herod Antipas, the women of Jerusalem and the penitent criminal; historians debate whether these come from separate sources or from Luke's shaping. Pilate's repeated wish to free Jesus is hard to square with his harsh record in Philo and Josephus, and many think Luke and the other Gospels softened him.
Read as Luke's case for Jesus' innocence

Luke builds the chapter like a court record: three times Pilate finds no case, Herod finds none, a criminal says he has done nothing out of place, and a Roman officer calls him righteous. The man truly guilty of revolt and murder goes free. For Luke's readers in the Roman world, the message was that Jesus died not as a criminal but as the innocent one of Isaiah's song, "counted with the lawless" (22:37).
Read as the death of a righteous martyr who forgives

Luke's Jesus dies as he lived: caring for others. He turns to the weeping women, prays for his executioners, opens paradise to a dying criminal and entrusts his spirit to his Father with a psalm of trust. Luke leaves out the cry "My God, my God, why have you abandoned me?" (Mark 15:34). The pattern returns in Stephen's death (Acts 7:59–60), a model for every Christian martyr.

views.H: Pilate, prefect from AD 26 to 36, came to Jerusalem at Passover with troops and heard cases himself. Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, was in the city for the feast; sending a prisoner to the ruler of his home region was a courtesy, not a legal duty. Crucifixion was Rome's punishment for slaves and rebels, carried out by soldiers outside the city, with the victim sometimes made to carry the crossbeam. The bones of a crucified man named Yehohanan, found in a Jerusalem tomb in 1968, show that a crucified Jew could be buried, as Jesus was. Rock-cut tombs with benches for the body ringed the city.
views.C: Luke follows Mark's outline of the trial and crucifixion but adds much: the three charges (23:2), Herod (23:6–12), the threefold verdict of innocence, the women of Jerusalem (23:27–31), the prayer for forgiveness (23:34, missing in some early manuscripts), the two criminals' conversation (23:39–43), the last words from Psalm 31, the centurion's "righteous," and the crowds' grief. Scholars debate whether a second passion source lies behind these, or Luke's own composition. Luke leaves out the scourging and crowning with thorns by Pilate's soldiers, the cry of Psalm 22, and Matthew's "His blood on us" (Matthew 27:25).
views.L: The chapter is a gallery of witnesses to Jesus' innocence, and a set of encounters in which people show who they are: Pilate weak, Herod curious and cruel, the crowd swayed, Simon made to follow, the women grieving, the rulers sneering, one criminal mocking and one asking, the centurion praising, Joseph faithful. Jesus' three sayings from the cross in Luke are all addressed to others or to the Father: forgiveness, promise, trust. "Today" returns (23:43), Luke's word for salvation arriving (2:11; 4:21; 19:9).
views.J: Luke distinguishes the leaders from the people: the people watch and then mourn (23:35, 48); women of Jerusalem lament; a member of the council dissents and gives Jesus a burial according to the Law, and the women keep the Sabbath. Yet Luke-Acts also says the people of Jerusalem asked for the crucifixion (23:13–23; Acts 3:13–15), and such passages were later used to accuse all Jews of killing Christ. The Catholic Church rejected that charge in 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4), and many churches have since; see the deep dive.
views.T: Luke's passion is read on Palm Sunday in Year C of the Roman and Revised Common Lectionaries. Three of the traditional "Seven Last Words" come only from Luke: "Father, forgive them," "Today you will be with me in paradise" and "Father, into your hands." The women of Jerusalem became the eighth Station of the Cross, and Simon of Cyrene the fifth. The penitent criminal, named Dismas in later legend, is honored as the first to enter paradise; his prayer, "Remember me," is sung in the Orthodox liturgy before communion.

deep.b:
Luke's account of the trial repeats one verdict. Pilate: "I find nothing to charge this man with" (23:4). Pilate again, after questioning him: nothing to support the charges, "nothing he has done deserves death" (23:14–15). Herod, by sending him back, agrees (23:15). Pilate a third time: "I have found nothing in him that deserves death" (23:22). A dying criminal: "This man, though, has done nothing out of place" (23:41). The centurion: "This man really was righteous" (23:47).

Acts tells Paul's trials the same way. The commander Claudius Lysias writes that Paul is charged with nothing deserving death or chains (Acts 23:29); the governor Festus finds he has done nothing deserving death (Acts 25:25); King Agrippa says he could have been set free (Acts 26:31–32). Both the master and the apostle face the Jewish leaders, a Roman governor and a Herod, and are found innocent by Rome.

An apology to Rome: Henry Cadbury and many since have read Luke-Acts in part as a defense of Christianity before Roman readers: the movement is not seditious. A theology of the innocent sufferer: others stress that Luke's Jesus is the righteous servant who dies for others, and that the verdicts make the injustice plain. A word to Christians: others again think Luke wrote to reassure believers who faced Roman courts that innocence and faithfulness, not revolt, were their path. The readings are not exclusive.

The deep dive at Matthew 27 discusses "His blood on us" and the wider question of responsibility. Luke-Acts poses it in its own way. Luke's Gospel shows the chief priests, scribes and rulers driving the case (22:2; 23:10, 13, 23, 35), Pilate yielding, Herod mocking, Roman soldiers doing the killing, and the people first favoring Jesus, then shouting for crucifixion, then going home in grief. In Acts, Peter tells a Jerusalem crowd, "you used the hands of men outside the law" to kill him (Acts 2:23), and says they acted in ignorance (Acts 3:17); the church prays that Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel gathered against Jesus (Acts 4:27).

Jack T. Sanders (1987) argued that Luke-Acts ends with the Jewish people as a whole rejected. Jacob Jervell argued the reverse: Luke tells of a divided Israel, many thousands of whom believed, and the church as Israel restored. Most readers see Luke's harsh words as a prophet's call to his own people, spoken by Jews to Jews, not a verdict on a race. Historically, Jesus was executed by Rome. Christians nonetheless used these texts for centuries to call Jews "Christ-killers"; the Catholic Church rejected the charge of collective guilt in 1965 (Nostra Aetate 4), and Jesus' prayer in 23:34 stands against every such use.

deep.h: "Father, forgive them": did scribes cut it out?
deep.b:
The prayer of 23:34 is missing from Papyrus 75 (about 175–225), Codex Vaticanus, the first hand of Bezae and other early witnesses in Egypt and the West; it is present in Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and most later manuscripts, and second-century writers seem to know it. The editors of the NA28 and SBL editions print it in double brackets.

Added: the saying may have been a true saying of Jesus passed on outside the Gospels and written into Luke later, perhaps under the influence of Stephen's prayer (Acts 7:60). Metzger's committee took this view, adding that the words bear marks of coming from Jesus himself. Removed: others, such as Nathan Eubank, argue that Luke wrote it, since it matches Luke's themes of ignorance and forgiveness (Acts 3:17; 13:27) and the parallel with Stephen is Luke's own design. Why remove it? Some second-century Christians saw the fall of Jerusalem as God's punishment of the Jews; a prayer for their forgiveness, which God had evidently not granted, may have seemed impossible. If so, the omission is an early trace of anti-Jewish feeling in the church. Metzger's committee thought this motive unlikely; Eubank argues for it.

Either way, the prayer has become one of the best-known words of Jesus, and a pattern for the martyrs.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the ones who waited
deep.b: Luke opens and closes Jesus' life with faithful Jews who are "waiting" (prosdechomai). At the beginning Simeon was looking forward to the comforting of Israel (2:25), and Anna spoke to all who were looking for Jerusalem to be redeemed (2:38). At the end Joseph of Arimathea, a council member who had not agreed with the verdict, was looking for the kingdom of God (23:51), and on the road two disciples say, "We had pinned our hopes on him" to redeem Israel (24:21). I suggest that Luke frames the story with this "waiting Israel" on purpose: the old man who takes the child in his arms and the old prophet who speaks of him at his birth (2:28, 38), and the council member who takes his body down at his death, are faces of the same faithful remnant, and Luke wants his readers to see that Jesus was received, at both ends, by Jews who had long waited for God. Commentators often note the link between Simeon and Joseph; reading it as a deliberate frame for the whole Gospel is my suggestion.

echoes: Psalm 2:1–2; Psalm 22:7; Psalm 22:18; Psalm 31:5; Psalm 38:11; Psalm 69:21; Isaiah 53:7; Isaiah 53:12; Hosea 10:8; Deuteronomy 21:22–23; Amos 8:9; Zechariah 12:10; Matthew 27:1–66; Mark 15:1–47; John 18:28–19:42; Acts 2:22–36; Acts 3:13–17; Acts 4:25–28; Acts 7:59–60; Acts 13:27–29
links: Sayings of Jesus on the cross
Sayings of Jesus on the cross

settings.by: the council: chief priests, elders and scribes; Pilate; Jesus
settings.to: Pilate, at his court in Jerusalem
settings.when: early in the morning after the council's hearing
settings.why: for the accusers, to turn a religious claim into a political charge a Roman governor would have to act on; for Pilate, to test whether Jesus was a rebel king
settings.readers: Luke's readers, often accused themselves of disturbing the peace (Acts 17:6–7; 24:5), saw that the charges against their Lord were false.

settings.by: Herod Antipas, with the chief priests and scribes accusing
settings.when: during Pilate's hearing, while Herod was in Jerusalem for Passover
settings.why: Pilate sought the opinion of the ruler of Galilee; Herod hoped to see a sign; Jesus' silence refused to entertain him
settings.readers: Readers saw the fulfillment of Psalm 2, rulers gathered against the Lord's anointed (Acts 4:25–27), and the friend of John's killer finding nothing against Jesus either.
views: Harold Hoehner and others defend the hearing as plausible and rooted in a source close to Herod's court (compare Joanna and Manaen, 8:3; Acts 13:1).
Martin Dibelius and others thought the scene grew from early Christian reading of Psalm 2.

settings.what: Pilate's verdict and the crowd's demand
settings.by: Pilate; the chief priests, the rulers and the people
settings.to: one another, at the governor's court
settings.when: after Herod sent Jesus back
settings.why: Pilate three times declared Jesus innocent and offered to flog and release him; the crowd, with the leaders, demanded Barabbas and the cross, and Pilate yielded
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw an innocent man condemned and a guilty one freed, the exchange Peter preaches in Acts 3:13–15.
views: The Gospels agree that Pilate tried to free Jesus.
Many historians think the Gospels softened Pilate, known from Philo and Josephus as harsh, as Christians came to live under Rome.

settings.to: the women of Jerusalem who followed him lamenting, and the crowd
settings.when: on the way to the place of execution
settings.why: to turn their grief toward the disaster coming on their city and children, as he had warned before (19:41–44; 21:20–24)
settings.readers: If Luke wrote after the Romans destroyed Jerusalem in AD 70, as most scholars think, his readers knew the prophecy had come true; if before, they heard it as a warning still ahead. Either way they heard Jesus grieving, not gloating, over the city.
views: Most read it as a prophecy of the siege and fall of Jerusalem.
Some see a wider warning of the last day, using the cry of Hosea 10:8 as Revelation 6:16 does.

settings.to: the Father, about those crucifying him
settings.when: as he was being crucified
settings.why: to ask forgiveness for those who acted without knowing what they did, practicing his own command to pray for those who abuse you (6:28)
settings.readers: The prayer became the pattern for Christian martyrs, beginning with Stephen (Acts 7:60), and a check on any hatred toward those blamed for Jesus' death.

settings.when: while he hung on the cross, with the people watching
settings.why: to ridicule a would-be Messiah and king who could not save himself
settings.readers: Readers heard the irony: the mockers spoke true titles (Messiah, Chosen One, King of the Jews), and he saved others precisely by not saving himself.

settings.what: The two criminals and the promise of paradise
settings.by: the two men crucified with Jesus; Jesus
settings.when: on the cross
settings.why: one criminal mocked; the other confessed his guilt, declared Jesus innocent and asked to be remembered in his kingdom; Jesus promised him paradise that very day
settings.readers: For Luke's readers the scene showed salvation given to the least deserving, at the last moment, by grace and faith, and "today" made the promise present.

settings.when: at the ninth hour, as he died
settings.why: to give his life into God's hands in the words of Psalm 31:5, a prayer of trust
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned how a believer dies; Stephen prays to Jesus in the same way (Acts 7:59).

settings.what: The centurion's verdict and the witnesses
settings.by: the centurion; the crowds; those who knew Jesus and the women from Galilee
settings.to: God, and to all who saw
settings.when: at Jesus' death
settings.why: the Roman officer praised God and declared Jesus righteous; the crowds went home grieving; his friends watched from a distance
settings.readers: Readers saw the last Roman verdict on Jesus, and the women who would witness the burial and the empty tomb.

settings.by: Joseph of Arimathea; the women from Galilee
settings.when: late on Friday, as the Sabbath began
settings.why: to give Jesus an honorable burial before the Sabbath, as the Law required for a hanged man (Deuteronomy 21:23), and to prepare spices for anointing after the Sabbath
settings.readers: Luke's readers saw that Jesus truly died and was buried in a known tomb, and that his followers remained faithful to the Law.

title: Their Eyes Were Opened
sum: At dawn on the first day of the week the women from Galilee come to the tomb with spices and find the stone rolled back and the body gone. Two men in flashing clothes ask them why they look for the living one among the dead, and remind them of Jesus' words in Galilee: the Son of Man must be handed over, crucified, and rise on the third day. The women, named as Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James and others, tell the Eleven, who dismiss it as nonsense. Peter runs to the tomb and sees only the linen wrappings.

Later that day two disciples walking to Emmaus are joined by a stranger, whom they do not recognize. They tell him of their dashed hope that Jesus would redeem Israel. He calls them slow of heart and, starting from Moses and all the prophets, explains the things about himself in the Scriptures. At supper he takes the bread, blesses, breaks and gives it, and their eyes are opened; he vanishes. They hurry back to Jerusalem to find the Eleven saying, "The Lord really has been raised! He has appeared to Simon."

As they talk, Jesus stands among them: "Peace to you." They think he is a spirit; he shows his hands and feet, invites them to touch him, and eats a piece of fish. He opens their minds to the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms, tells them that repentance and forgiveness must be proclaimed in his name to all nations starting from Jerusalem, and promises to send the Father's promise. He leads them out toward Bethany, lifts his hands and blesses them, and is carried up into heaven. They bow down before him, return to Jerusalem with great joy, and are continually in the temple, blessing God.
readings: All four Gospels agree that women found Jesus' tomb empty on the first day of the week, and Paul lists appearances to Peter, the Twelve and others (1 Corinthians 15:3–8). Historians who accept the resurrection as an event, such as N. T. Wright, point to the empty tomb and the appearances together as the best explanation of the rise of the faith; others, such as Dale Allison, weigh the evidence more cautiously, and skeptical scholars explain the appearances as visions. Luke's details differ from the other Gospels: two men (as John has two angels), where Mark and Matthew have one; all appearances near Jerusalem; and, in the Gospel, the ascension apparently on Easter day.

Luke ends where he began, in the temple, with blessing and joy. The chapter is built in three scenes, tomb, road and room, each moving from confusion to understanding through remembering Jesus' words and hearing the Scriptures opened. The risen Lord explains that everything written about him had to be fulfilled, and points ahead to Acts: witnesses, the Spirit, all nations.
Read as the church at worship

Emmaus has the shape of Christian worship: the Scriptures opened, then bread taken, blessed, broken and given, and the Lord known "in the breaking of the bread." Luke's readers met on the first day of the week for exactly this (Acts 20:7), and many churches still read the Emmaus story at Easter as a picture of their own Sunday gathering.

views.H: Jewish burial customs, women anointing a body with spices after the Sabbath, the first day of the week, and a village a few miles from Jerusalem, all fit the setting. Emmaus has not been certainly identified (see the note at 24:13). Ancient law gave women's testimony little weight, which many historians take as evidence that the Gospels did not invent the women as first witnesses. Bethany lay on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, about two miles from the city.
views.C: Luke rewrites Mark's tomb story so that the angels point back to Galilee rather than forward to it (compare Mark 16:7), and he keeps every appearance in Jerusalem, where Acts will begin. The Emmaus story and the meal of fish are Luke's own. Several phrases in 24:3–52 are missing from Codex Bezae and Old Latin manuscripts, the "Western non-interpolations"; most editors now print the longer text, but the SBL edition follows the shorter at 24:3 and 24:36 (see the deep dive). Acts 1 retells the ending with forty days of appearances, which raises the question of how the two accounts fit.
views.L: Three scenes, each a movement from not seeing to seeing. The women remember (24:8); the travelers' eyes are opened (24:31); the disciples' minds are opened (24:45). The verb "open" links the eyes, the Scriptures and the minds. Meals frame the recognition, as meals have framed the whole Gospel. The last words are blessing, joy and worship, matching the first chapters' songs and the temple where the story began.
views.J: Every character is Jewish, and the hope is Israel's: "We had pinned our hopes on him as the man who would redeem Israel" (24:21). Jesus reads his story from Moses, the Prophets and the Psalms, the three parts of the Jewish Scriptures. The disciples end in the temple, praising Israel's God. Jewish readers have answered the claim that the Scriptures foretold a suffering and rising Messiah by reading those passages of Israel or of other figures; the conversation between the two readings goes back to this chapter.
views.T: The church reads this chapter at Easter and on the Feast of the Ascension, forty days later, following Acts. The Emmaus meal is often painted (Caravaggio's Supper at Emmaus, 1601; Rembrandt's of 1648). Henry Francis Lyte's hymn "Abide with Me" (1847) grew from the travelers' plea, "Abide with us" in the King James Version. Luke 24:44 is cited in debates about which books make up the Old Testament (see the card below), and the ascension and blessing shaped the creeds: "he ascended into heaven, and is seated at the right hand of the Father."

deep.b:
Codex Bezae (D, about 400) and the Old Latin manuscripts usually have a longer text than other manuscripts, with added details. But in a handful of places near the end of Luke they have a shorter one. In 1881 B. F. Westcott and F. J. A. Hort argued that in these places the "Western" text had escaped additions that crept into all the others. Since they would not call the longer readings "Western interpolations," they gave the shorter readings an awkward name: "Western non-interpolations." They listed nine: Matthew 27:49 and, in Luke, 22:19b–20 (the cup after supper), 24:3 ("of the Lord Jesus"), 24:6 ("He isn't here, but he has been raised"), 24:12 (Peter at the tomb), 24:36 ("and said to them, Peace to you"), 24:40 (the hands and feet), 24:51 ("and was carried up into heaven") and 24:52 ("they bowed down before him"). They printed the longer words in double brackets.

For eighty years many editions and some English Bibles, the RSV among them, followed Westcott and Hort in several of these places. Then in 1961 Papyrus 75 was published: a copy of Luke and John made about 175–225, a century and more older than Bezae. It has the longer text in every one of these passages. Klyne Snodgrass (1972) argued that the shorter readings are omissions, some accidental, some by scribes tidying the text. The UBS and Nestle-Aland editions since the 1970s print the longer text in all of them. Bart Ehrman has argued the opposite case for several: that the longer readings were added by second-century scribes to stress that Jesus' body was real, his death atoning and his ascension bodily, against teachers who denied these.

This translation follows the longer text throughout, with Papyrus 75, NA28 and Tyndale House. At 24:3 and 24:36 the SBL edition, which follows Westcott and Hort more closely, has the shorter reading; the variant notes say so. Each place has its own variant entry with the witnesses.

deep.h: One long Easter day, and forty days in Acts
deep.b:
Read on its own, Luke 24 seems to happen in a single day: the women come at dawn (24:1), the two walk to Emmaus "on that same day" (24:13), they return "that very hour" (24:33), Jesus appears while they are talking (24:36), and then, without a break, he leads them out to Bethany and is carried up (24:50–51). The same author begins Acts by saying Jesus appeared to them "for forty days" before he was taken up (Acts 1:3).

Compression: many readers think the Gospel simply summarizes, as ancient historians often did; the teaching of 24:44–49 may sum up the forty days, and the ascension closes the volume. Theology: others think Luke uses Easter day in the Gospel to join resurrection and exaltation as one event, and forty days in Acts, the number of Israel's wilderness years and Jesus' testing, to mark a time of preparation. New information: some critical scholars think Luke learned or shaped the forty-day account after writing the Gospel.

Luke also keeps all the appearances near Jerusalem, while Matthew and John tell of appearances in Galilee (Matthew 28:16–20; John 21). Paul's list adds an appearance to more than five hundred at once and one to James (1 Corinthians 15:6–7). The Gospels do not try to harmonize; each tells the story for its own purpose, and Luke's purpose is to show the message going out from Jerusalem.

deep.h: Word and table on the road to Emmaus
deep.b:
The Emmaus story (24:13–35) is a small masterpiece. It moves from Jerusalem and back, from sadness to burning hearts, from not recognizing to recognizing. At its center is the travelers' speech (24:19–24), a summary of the gospel by people who do not yet believe it: a prophet mighty in deed and word, crucified, the tomb found empty, angels saying he is alive, "but they did not see him." Then the stranger interprets the Scriptures, and at table he takes, blesses, breaks and gives the bread, the four actions of the feeding (9:16) and the Last Supper (22:19).

Luke's readers would recognize their own Sunday gathering: the Scriptures read and explained, then the bread broken. The two report how he was known to them "in the breaking of the bread" (24:35), Luke's phrase for the church's meals (Acts 2:42). The story teaches that the risen Lord, no longer seen, is still met in word and table. It also teaches humility: the disciples who knew Jesus best did not recognize him until he opened their eyes.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the firstborn who opens
deep.b: Luke uses the verb dianoigō, "to open fully," four times in his Gospel. Three are in this chapter: their eyes were opened (24:31), he laid open the Scriptures (24:32), he opened their minds (24:45). The fourth is at the presentation in the temple, quoting the law: "Every male that opens a womb will be called holy" (2:23). I suggest Luke means a link: the firstborn who "opened the womb" and was presented as holy to the Lord at the beginning is the risen one who opens eyes, Scriptures and minds at the end, the "firstborn from the dead" (Colossians 1:18). Both scenes are set around the temple, and both end in blessing God (2:28; 24:53). Many commentators note the threefold opening in chapter 24; the link to 2:23 is my suggestion and rests on the shared verb.

echoes: Genesis 3:7; Leviticus 9:22; Deuteronomy 18:15; Psalm 16:10; Psalm 39:3; Isaiah 32:15; Isaiah 49:6; Isaiah 53:12; Hosea 6:2; 2 Kings 2:9–15; Sirach 50:20–21; Matthew 28:1–20; Mark 16:1–20; John 20:1–29; John 21:1–14; Acts 1:1–14; Acts 2:42; Acts 10:40–43; 1 Corinthians 15:3–8

settings.what: The two men at the tomb
settings.when: at dawn on the first day of the week, inside the empty tomb
settings.why: to tell them Jesus was alive and to make them remember his own predictions of his death and rising
settings.readers: Luke's readers learned that faith begins by remembering Jesus' words, and that women were the first to hear the news.
views: Mark has one young man inside the tomb (Mark 16:5), Matthew one angel sitting on the stone (Matthew 28:2–5), and John two angels seen by Mary Magdalene (John 20:12).

settings.by: Mary Magdalene, Joanna, Mary the mother of James and the other women
settings.to: the Eleven and all the rest
settings.when: on their return from the tomb
settings.why: to tell what they had found and heard; the apostles dismissed it as nonsense
settings.readers: Readers saw the apostles' disbelief honestly recorded, and the women's witness vindicated.

settings.what: The road to Emmaus: the travelers' story and the stranger's lesson
settings.by: Cleopas and his companion; Jesus, unrecognized
settings.when: later on Easter day, on the road from Jerusalem
settings.why: the travelers poured out their disappointed hope; Jesus showed them from Moses and the prophets that the Messiah had to suffer and enter his glory
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who had not seen Jesus, learned that the Scriptures read in his light, and the breaking of bread, are where he is met.
views: Luke does not say. Suggestions include Cleopas' wife (if Cleopas is the Clopas of John 19:25) or another disciple; the anonymity lets each reader take the second place.

settings.by: the two travelers; the Eleven and those with them
settings.when: that same evening
settings.why: to share the news: the Lord had appeared to Simon, and had been known in the breaking of the bread
settings.readers: The Eleven's words echo one of the oldest Christian creeds (1 Corinthians 15:3–5), the confession Luke's readers knew.

settings.what: "Peace to you": the appearance to the disciples
settings.to: the Eleven and those with them
settings.when: Easter evening, in Jerusalem
settings.why: to calm their fear, show that he was no ghost but risen in body, and restore them to fellowship at table
settings.readers: Luke's readers, who may already have heard teachers say Christ only seemed to have a body, received the evidence: hands, feet, flesh and bones, and a meal.

settings.what: The last teaching and the commission
settings.to: the Eleven and those with them
settings.when: after the meal (in Acts, during the forty days)
settings.why: to open their minds to the Scriptures, to give them the message of repentance and forgiveness for all nations, to name them witnesses, and to tell them to wait in the city for the Father's promise
settings.readers: This is the bridge to Acts. Luke's readers, Gentiles among them, saw their own faith as the fulfillment of this command, beginning from Jerusalem.

settings.when: near Bethany, on the Mount of Olives
settings.why: Jesus lifted his hands and blessed them like a priest, and was carried up into heaven; they bowed down before him and returned to the temple to bless God
settings.readers: Luke's Gospel ends as it began, in the temple, with God's people blessing God and full of joy.
views: Read alone, the Gospel seems to place the departure on Easter evening.
Acts 1:3 places it after forty days; most readers think the Gospel compresses the time.

traditions.q: Jesus speaks of what was written "in the Law of Moses, in the Prophets and in the Psalms" (24:44). Which books make up the Old Testament?
views: The Old Testament is the Hebrew Bible's thirty-nine books; "the books commonly called Apocrypha, not being of divine inspiration, are no part of the canon of the Scripture" (Westminster Confession 1.3). Reformed writers point to Jesus' threefold division and to Josephus' list of twenty-two books (Against Apion 1.38–41) as evidence of a closed Hebrew canon in Jesus' day.

The church received the Old Testament as the apostles used it, largely in the Greek translation, and the Council of Trent defined forty-six books, including Tobit, Judith, Wisdom, Sirach, Baruch and 1–2 Maccabees (Session 4, 1546; Catechism 120). Jesus' phrase names the parts of Scripture without listing its books.

The Orthodox Old Testament follows the Septuagint and includes the deuterocanonical books and some others, such as 1 Esdras, 3 Maccabees and Psalm 151; the Synod of Jerusalem (1672) affirmed several of them as Scripture. Some Orthodox theologians call these books "readable" and place them a step below the Hebrew canon.

The Articles list the Hebrew canon and say that the other books the church reads "for example of life and instruction of manners; but yet doth it not apply them to establish any doctrine" (Article 6).
The Ethiopian church has the widest Old Testament, including 1 Enoch and Jubilees, which no church outside the Ethiopian and Eritrean Orthodox tradition counts as Scripture.
